h1: Pastry stouts and dessert beers and how brewers build them
title: Pastry Stouts and Dessert Beers | Craft Beer School
desc: What a pastry stout is, which adjuncts brewers use, how they keep a dessert beer from tasting like syrup and how to enjoy one responsibly.
teaser: Vanilla, cacao, coffee, coconut. A pastry stout tastes like dessert in a glass. It takes careful brewing to stop there.
standfirst: Pastry stouts are big, dark, sweet beers loaded with dessert flavours: vanilla, chocolate, coffee, coconut, maple or cinnamon. They divide opinion and pack a lot of alcohol. Here is what they are, how brewers build them and how to taste one well.
sections:
A pastry stout is usually an imperial stout, often 9 to 12% ABV or more, with added ingredients that make it taste like a dessert. The name is informal and not an official style. Brewers use it for beers that aim to taste like brownies, tiramisu, s'mores, cookies or ice cream sundaes.

The base matters. Imperial stout is already rich, roasty and full-bodied, with chocolate, coffee and dark fruit flavours from roasted malts. Our imperial stout guide covers it. A pastry stout takes that base and pushes it further towards sweetness.

• Vanilla. Whole pods or extract, for a creamy, sweet aroma.
  • Cacao nibs. Roasted cocoa bean pieces, for real chocolate flavour without much sugar.
  • Coffee. Whole beans or cold brew, added late for fresh coffee aroma.
  • Lactose. Milk sugar, which yeast cannot ferment, for extra sweetness and body.
  • Coconut, maple syrup, cinnamon, nuts or fruit. Each brewer picks a combination to suggest a particular dessert.

In India, brewers have good local options. Coffee from Chikmagalur and Coorg, cacao from Kerala and Karnataka, coconut from the coast and spices from almost anywhere. Our guide to adding coffee to beer explains how brewers handle it.

The challenge is sweetness. A pastry stout needs a high original gravity for its strength. Brewers often mash at a higher temperature, around 68 to 70 °C, to leave more unfermentable sugars for body. Lactose adds more. Finishing gravities can be high, sometimes above 1.030, which is far sweeter than most beers.

To stop that tipping into syrup, good brewers lean on roast bitterness, hop bitterness and alcohol warmth. The roasted malts give a dry, slightly bitter edge. Cacao nibs and coffee add bitterness without sugar. The goal is a beer that tastes like dessert but finishes clean enough to take another sip.

Adjuncts usually go in after fermentation, in the conditioning tank, where brewers can taste and adjust. Vanilla and coffee in particular are easy to overdo and impossible to remove.

Many pastry stouts are also aged in used spirit barrels, most often bourbon or whisky casks. The wood adds vanilla, coconut and caramel notes of its own, along with some of the spirit soaked into the staves. That is why barrel-aged stouts and pastry stouts often share a menu: the barrel does part of the dessert work. Ageing takes months. Some barrels go wrong, so these beers are expensive to make and usually released in small batches.

In India's heat, barrel ageing moves faster and loses more beer to evaporation than in a cool cellar, so brewers who try it watch their barrels closely.

Some drinkers love pastry stouts as rich, indulgent treats. Others feel they taste more like a milkshake than a beer, or that the adjuncts hide the brewing. Both views have a point. A well-made pastry stout is balanced, with the base beer still present under the dessert flavours. A poorly made one tastes like sweet syrup with a hint of alcohol.

The best way to judge is to ask whether the beer would still be good without the adjuncts. If the stout underneath is excellent, the additions are seasoning. If it is not, they are a disguise.

Pastry stouts suit dessert, or replace it. Try one with gulab jamun, chocolate cake, coffee-flavoured desserts or a plain vanilla ice cream. Our guide to beer and dessert pairing has more ideas. Serve around 10 to 13 °C, warmer than a lager, so the aromas open up, in a small tulip or snifter glass.

A 12% pastry stout carries well over twice the alcohol of a standard lager in the same volume. The sweetness can hide it. Treat it as something to sip and share. Order a small tasting measure, split a bottle among friends and drink water alongside. Many taprooms serve these beers in 150 to 200 ml pours for exactly this reason.

Tasting a pastry stout well is a useful exercise. Look for how many separate flavours you can name, whether the sweetness is balanced by roast and bitterness and how clean the finish is. Those are the same questions a trained taster asks of any beer.
faqs: Is pastry stout an official beer style?
No. Pastry stout is an informal name for sweet imperial stouts with dessert-like additions such as vanilla, cacao, coffee and lactose. Competitions usually judge them in specialty categories.
Why are pastry stouts so strong?
Most are built on an imperial stout base, which needs a lot of malt for its rich body. That usually means 9 to 12% ABV or more.
What temperature should I serve a pastry stout?
Around 10 to 13 °C. Warmer than lager lets the vanilla, chocolate and coffee aromas open up.
